claim: AWS Organizations lets you centrally manage and govern many accounts: create accounts, group them, apply policies for governance, and pay for all of them with a single payment method.
question: What is AWS Organizations, and what does it let an administrator manage centrally?

values.display: centrally manage and govern your environment
a single payment method for all of your accounts
apply policies for governance

evidence.quote: AWS Organizations helps you centrally manage and govern your environment as you grow and scale your AWS resources. Using Organizations, you can create accounts and allocate resources, group accounts to organize your workflows, apply policies for governance, and simplify billing by using a single payment method for all of your accounts.

claim: CloudTrail activated across the accounts of an organization creates a log of all activity that member accounts cannot turn off or modify.
question: Can a member account turn off or modify the CloudTrail log that the organization activates across accounts?

values.display: cannot be turned off or modified by member accounts
a log of all activity

qualifiers.scope: CloudTrail activated across the accounts of an organization

evidence.quote: You can activate AWS CloudTrail across accounts, which creates a log of all activity in your cloud environment that cannot be turned off or modified by member accounts.

claim: All features is the default feature set of AWS Organizations, and it includes every capability of consolidated billing plus the administrative capabilities.
question: Which feature set does a new organization use by default, and what does it include?

values.display: the default feature set
all the capabilities of consolidated billing

evidence.quote: All features is the default feature set that is available to AWS Organizations.
All features mode provides all the capabilities of consolidated billing along with the administrative capabilities.

claim: With only the consolidated billing feature set, an organization cannot integrate other AWS services across its accounts and cannot use policies to restrict what users and roles in its accounts can do.
question: What can an organization with only the consolidated billing feature set not do?

values.display: you can't enable other AWS services to integrate
use policies to restrict what users and roles

qualifiers.scope: organization with the consolidated billing feature set only

evidence.quote: For example, you can't enable other AWS services to integrate with your organization to work across all of its accounts, or use policies to restrict what users and roles in different accounts can do.

claim: An organization that started with consolidated billing can later enable all features, but once all features is enabled it cannot go back to consolidated billing.
question: Can an organization switch from all features back to consolidated billing only?

values.display: you can later enable all features
you cannot migrate from all features to consolidated billing

evidence.quote: If you create an organization with the consolidated billing feature set, you can later enable all features. However, you cannot migrate from all features to consolidated billing after all features is enabled.

claim: To enable all features, every invited member account must approve the change by accepting a request; accounts created with AWS Organizations get no request.
question: Which member accounts must approve the switch to all features?

values.display: Every invited account must approve enabling all features
don't get a request

qualifiers.scope: organization moving from consolidated billing to all features

evidence.quote: Every invited account must approve enabling all features by accepting the request.
Accounts that you created using AWS Organizations don't get a request because they don't need to approve the additional control.

claim: An organization is a collection of AWS accounts arranged in a tree, with a root at the top and organizational units nested under the root.
question: How does AWS define an organization and its structure?

values.display: a collection of AWS accounts
hierarchical, tree-like structure
a root at the top

evidence.quote: An organization is a collection of AWS accounts that you can manage centrally and organize into a hierarchical, tree-like structure with a root at the top and organizational units nested under the root.

claim: An organizational unit (OU) is a group of AWS accounts in an organization, and an OU can contain other OUs to form a hierarchy.
question: What is an organizational unit (OU)?

values.display: a group of AWS accounts within an organization
An OU can also contain other OUs

evidence.quote: An organizational unit (OU) is a group of AWS accounts within an organization. An OU can also contain other OUs enabling you to create a hierarchy.

claim: Nested OUs inherit the policies of their parent OU in addition to any controls attached directly to them.
question: Does a nested OU receive the policies of its parent OU?

values.display: inherit the policies from the parent OU
in addition to any controls assigned directly

evidence.quote: These OUs inherit the policies from the parent OU in addition to any controls assigned directly to the team-level OU.

claim: You cannot change which account in an organization is the management account.
question: Can the management account of an organization be changed to another account?

values.display: You cannot change which account
is the management account

evidence.quote: You cannot change which account in your organization is the management account.

claim: The management account is the payer account: it pays all charges that the accounts in its organization accrue.
question: Which account pays for the usage of the member accounts in an organization?

values.display: the role of a payer account
responsible for paying all charges

evidence.quote: This account has the role of a payer account and is responsible for paying all charges accrued by the accounts in its organization.

claim: A member account can belong to only one organization at a time.
question: Can one AWS account be a member of more than one organization at the same time?

values.display: only one organization at a time
A member account can belong to

evidence.quote: A member account can belong to only one organization at a time.

claim: Only the management account can create member accounts or invite existing accounts to join the organization; a delegated administrator account cannot.
question: Which account can create member accounts and invite existing accounts into an organization?

values.display: can be done only from the management account
not from a delegated administrator account

evidence.quote: Creating member accounts and inviting existing accounts to join the organization can be done only from the management account, not from a delegated administrator account.

claim: A declarative policy attached to the root applies to all OUs and accounts including the management account, while an authorization policy such as an SCP attached to the root does not apply to the management account.
question: Does a policy attached to the root apply to the management account?

values.display: including the management account for the organization
It does not apply to the management account

qualifiers.scope: policies attached to the organization root

evidence.quote: If you apply a declarative policy to the root, it applies to all organizational units (OUs) and accounts, including the management account for the organization.

If you apply an authorization policy (for example, a service control policy (SCP)), to the root, it applies to all organizational units (OUs) and member accounts in the organization. It does not apply to the management account in the organization.

claim: Registering a member account as delegated administrator for an AWS service gives it some administrative permissions for that service plus read-only Organizations permissions, which reduces use of the management account.
question: What is a delegated administrator account, and why use it instead of the management account?

values.display: reduce the usage of the management account
some administrative permissions for that service
permissions for Organizations read-only actions

qualifiers.scope: member account registered as delegated administrator for one AWS service
qualifiers.condition: the service supports delegated administrators and trusted access is enabled

evidence.quote: Many AWS services that integrate with Organizations enable you to reduce the usage of the management account.

By registering a member account as a delegated administrator for an AWS service you enable that account to have some administrative permissions for that service, as well as permissions for Organizations read-only actions.

claim: AWS recommends keeping all resources out of the management account, because SCPs do not restrict any users or roles in the management account.
question: Why does AWS recommend running no workloads in the management account?

values.display: keep them out of the management account
SCPs do not work to restrict any users or roles

evidence.quote: Store all of your AWS resources in other AWS accounts in the organization and keep them out of the management account. One important reason to keep your resources in other accounts is because Organizations service control policies (SCPs) do not work to restrict any users or roles in the management account.

claim: Member accounts can leave the organization or close themselves, so AWS recommends an SCP at the root that denies organizations:LeaveOrganization and account:CloseAccount.
question: How can an organization stop member accounts from leaving or closing themselves without approval?

values.display: Member accounts can leave your organization or close themselves
attach an SCP at the root
organizations:LeaveOrganization and account:CloseAccount

evidence.quote: Member accounts can leave your organization or close themselves, which can disrupt governance, billing, and security controls.

We recommend that you attach an SCP at the root of your organization that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization and account:CloseAccount actions to prevent member accounts from performing these actions without approval from the management account or a delegated administrator.

claim: An account can be removed from an organization only if it has what a standalone account needs: a support plan, verified contact information and a current payment method.
question: What must a member account have before it can be removed and stand alone?

values.display: only if the account has the information
provide a current payment method

qualifiers.scope: member account being removed from an organization

evidence.quote: You can remove an account from your organization only if the account has the information that is required for it to operate as a standalone account.
For each account that you want to make standalone, you must choose a support plan, provide and verify the required contact information, and provide a current payment method.

claim: After an account leaves an organization, its principals are no longer affected by any organization policy, so SCP restrictions are gone and its users and roles might have more permissions.
question: What happens to SCP restrictions when an account leaves an organization?

values.display: restrictions imposed by SCPs are gone
might have more permissions than they had before

qualifiers.scope: account removed from or leaving an organization

evidence.quote: The principals in the account are no longer affected by any policies that applied in the organization. This means that restrictions imposed by SCPs are gone, and the users and roles in the account might have more permissions than they had before.

claim: When a member account is removed, the IAM role that gave the management account access is not deleted automatically; to end that access you must delete the role by hand.
question: Is the management account's access role deleted when a member account leaves the organization?

values.display: isn't automatically deleted
you must manually delete the IAM role

evidence.quote: When you remove a member account from the organization, any IAM role that was created to enable access by the organization's management account isn't automatically deleted. If you want to terminate this access from the former organization's management account, then you must manually delete the IAM role.

claim: An account that is a delegated administrator for any AWS service enabled for the organization cannot be removed until it is deregistered.
question: Can a delegated administrator account be removed from the organization?

values.display: must not be a delegated administrator account
you must first deregister it

qualifiers.scope: member account being removed from an organization
qualifiers.condition: the account is a delegated administrator

evidence.quote: The account that you want to remove must not be a delegated administrator account for any AWS service enabled for your organization. If the account is a delegated administrator, you must first deregister it (or change the delegated administrator to another account that is remaining in the organization) before you can remove it.

claim: An account created in the organization can be removed only 4 days or more after it was created; invited accounts have no waiting period.
question: How long after creation can an account created in an organization be removed?

values.display: at least four days
Invited accounts aren't subject to this waiting period

evidence.quote: To remove an account that you created in the organization, you must wait until at least four days after the account was created. Invited accounts aren't subject to this waiting period.

claim: When you create an account in an organization, AWS Organizations creates an IAM role in it that is named OrganizationAccountAccessRole by default, and no other users or roles.
question: Which IAM role does Organizations create in a new member account?

values.display: OrganizationAccountAccessRole
automatically creates an IAM role
doesn't create any other users or roles

qualifiers.scope: member account created through AWS Organizations
qualifiers.condition: a different name can be given at creation

evidence.quote: When you create an account in your organization, in addition to the root user, AWS Organizations automatically creates an IAM role that is by default named OrganizationAccountAccessRole. You can specify a different name when you create it, however we recommend that you name it consistently across all of your accounts. AWS Organizations doesn't create any other users or roles.

claim: An invited account does not get the access role automatically; after it accepts the invitation, an administrator can choose to create an IAM role that lets the management account access it.
question: Does an invited account get the OrganizationAccountAccessRole automatically?

values.display: you can then choose to create an IAM role
Organizations did not automatically create such a role

qualifiers.scope: existing account invited to the organization
qualifiers.condition: after the account accepts the invitation

evidence.quote: If you invite an existing account to join your organization and the account accepts the invitation, you can then choose to create an IAM role that allows the management account to access the invited member account.
If the account was invited to join, then Organizations did not automatically create such a role, but you or another administrator might have created one to get the same benefits.
